result.summary: Pausanias describes Lycosura, the oldest town, and Mount Lycæus, where Zeus was said to be reared. He lists its shrines, springs, rain rite, shadowless enclosure, rivers and the Nomia hills.

scenes.title: Lycosura and Zeus's Nurses
scenes.summary: Lycosura is called the oldest town; Mount Lycæus is said to be where Zeus was reared by the Nymphs Thisoa, Neda and Hagno.

scenes.title: Rain Rite and Pan's Temple
scenes.summary: The priest of Lycæan Zeus raises rain by stirring the spring Hagno. Pan's temple and hippodrome stand on the mountain.

scenes.title: Wonders of Lycæan Zeus
scenes.summary: The forbidden enclosure shows no shadows and entering it means death within a year. The altar and the Apollo festival are described.
scenes.stakes: Anyone entering the enclosure is said to die within a year.

scenes.title: Thisoa, Rivers and Nomia
scenes.summary: Rivers of the Thisoa district are listed, with three rivers named Achelous. The Nomia hills hold a temple of Pan Nomius.

alias_notes.explanation: Some Arcadians call the mountain Olympus or the Sacred Hill.
Apollo of the Lycæus temple is also called Pythian Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Bold claim that Lycosura is the oldest town and model for all cities.

analysis.text: Arcadians claim sacred priority, saying Zeus was born and reared on their mountain and not in Crete.
Pausanias reports local tradition and taboo, and declines to pry into secret rites.

legacy.text: Mount Lycæus and its Lycæan games are linked to the Arcadian cult of Zeus, and the name relates to the word lycanthropy via the Lycaon tradition.

fun_facts.text: Excavations at Mount Lykaion have found an ash altar with votive offerings dating back to prehistoric times.

language_notes.text: Cretans claimed Zeus was born and reared on Crete; Arcadians contest this by placing 'Crete' on Mount Lycæus, a local rival tradition.
The Ister is the Danube, thought to flow at a steady volume in all seasons.
An elegiac couplet is a two-line verse form in alternating long and short lines, often used for inscriptions.
At Syene (modern Aswan) the midsummer sun stands overhead when in Cancer, so objects cast no noon shadow there.
Homer's Iliad calls Achelous the greatest of rivers in passing, and the Niobe legend places her weeping stone on Sipylus.
Nomius means 'of pastures' (or 'of laws'); Pan Nomius is Pan as god of pastures.

context_notes.text: Pausanias repeats the Arcadians' own claim of great antiquity; it is local tradition, not established fact.
Rain-making by stirring a sacred spring is a sympathetic magic rite; Pausanias reports it without explaining the mechanism.
Pausanias elsewhere says that anyone who entered the precinct was said to be stoned or to die within the year.

literary_notes.text: The shadowless beasts create an eerie, supernatural picture, and the baffled hunter makes the sacred place's power concrete.
Pausanias sets the natural shadowless noon at Syene against the permanent marvel on Lycæus, making the latter seem more wondrous.
The author's pious reticence about the rites shows his reverent, personal tone and heightens the secrecy.
